title: Electric current and circuits
summary: Current, resistance, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, and batteries.
cards.0.p: The charge that passes through a cross-section per unit time is called current. Current is found with I = q/t, and its unit is the ampere (C/s). The direction of conventional current is opposite to the direction the electrons flow.
cards.0.key: In a metal wire, electrons carry the charge. If 20 C of charge passes through the cross-section in 10 seconds, the current is 2 A.
cards.1.p: What makes charges move is a potential difference. It is also called voltage, and its unit is the volt (J/C). Sources such as a battery convert another form of energy into electrical energy and maintain this difference.
cards.1.key: Two conditions are needed for a current. There must be a potential difference, and the circuit must be closed.
cards.1.once.soru: You connected a battery to a bulb, but one of the wires is broken. Does the bulb light up?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The circuit must be closed for a current. Charge cannot pass through a broken wire.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: No current flows at all while the circuit is open.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: There is a voltage here, but no closed path. So no current forms.
cards.2.p: A material's opposition to current is called resistance, and its unit is the ohm. The resistance of a wire is found with R = ρ·L/A. Resistance increases as the length grows and decreases as the cross-section grows. ρ is the resistivity, which depends on the material.
cards.2.svg#7: in metals, R rises as temperature rises
cards.2.key: Resistivity also depends on temperature. In metals, resistance increases as temperature increases. If a wire is drawn out to twice its length, its cross-section is halved and its resistance becomes 4 times as large.
cards.3.h: Ohm's law and the V–I graph
cards.3.p: In a metal wire at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = I·R. The V–I graph of this wire is a straight line, and its slope gives R. A bulb that heats up, however, is not ohmic.
cards.3.key: As the bulb's filament heats up, its resistance increases and its graph curves. The bulb's resistance is small when it is cold. That is why a bulb draws its largest current at the moment it is switched on.
cards.4.p: In the battery symbol, the long line is the + terminal and the short line is the − terminal. A bulb is shown as a cross inside a circle. An ammeter, which measures current, is shown as an A inside a circle, and a voltmeter, which measures voltage, as a V inside a circle.
cards.4.svg#10: long line: + terminal, short line: − terminal
cards.4.key: A resistor is drawn as a box or a zigzag. The resistance of connecting wires is usually taken as zero.
cards.4.once.soru: In a circuit diagram, which terminal does the long line of the battery show?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The long line is the + terminal, and the short line is the − terminal.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The short line is the − terminal.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: In a diagram, the terminals are told apart by line length.
cards.5.p: If resistors are connected so that they form a single path, this is called a series connection. The same current passes through all of them. The voltage is shared in proportion to the resistances: Req = R₁ + R₂.
cards.5.key: The larger resistor gets the larger voltage.
cards.5.once.soru: You add a third bulb in series to two bulbs in series. How do the bulbs glow?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: The equivalent resistance increases and the current decreases. So each bulb glows dimmer.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: A bulb added in series increases the resistance and decreases the current.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Since the total resistance changes, the current changes too.
cards.6.p: A resistor whose resistance can be adjusted with a slider is called a rheostat. The slider changes the length of wire the current passes through. If the wire gets longer, the resistance increases and the current in the circuit decreases.
cards.6.key: The potentiometer in a volume knob works the same way.
cards.6.svg#4: slider: L up → R up → I down → dim lamp
cards.6.once.soru: You increase the resistance of a rheostat in series with a lamp. What happens to the lamp?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The resistance of the circuit increases, and the current decreases.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: When resistance increases, the current decreases and the lamp dims.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The rheostat is in series with the lamp. So the current passes through both.
cards.7.p: If resistors are connected between the same two points on separate branches, this is called a parallel connection. All of them have the same voltage. The current is shared in inverse proportion to resistance: 1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
cards.7.key: For two resistors, Req = R₁·R₂/(R₁ + R₂). In a parallel connection, the equivalent resistance is smaller than even the smallest branch resistance. The wiring in homes is connected in parallel.
cards.7.etk.soru: Connect two resistors in parallel. Which branch carries more current?
cards.8.p: If the ends of a resistor are joined by a wire with no resistance, the current passes through the wire, not the resistor. This is called a short circuit. If the two ends of a battery are joined, a very large current flows in the circuit.
cards.8.key: No current passes through a resistor that has no potential difference across its ends. In a short circuit, the battery heats up. That is why fuses are used.
cards.8.once.soru: You join the two ends of a bulb with a wire that has no resistance. What happens to the bulb?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The current chooses the zero-resistance wire and skips the bulb.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The current skips the bulb and passes through the zero-resistance wire.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The ends of the bulb are now at the same potential. So no current passes through the bulb.
cards.9.h: A mixed circuit, step by step
cards.9.p: You solve a mixed circuit from the inside out. First you reduce the parallel groups to a single resistor, then you add the series resistors. You find the main current with I = V/Req. After that, you calculate the voltages and the branch currents.
cards.9.key: Check the result. The sum of the voltages across the series parts must equal the battery voltage.
cards.9.etk.soru: Put the steps in the right order for solving a mixed circuit.
cards.9.etk.ogeler.3: Find the voltage of each part
cards.10.p: Points connected by a wire with no resistance between them are at the same potential. No current passes through a resistor whose ends are at the same potential, so it can be removed from the circuit.
cards.10.key: These points can be merged into a single point in the diagram. In a balanced bridge (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄), no current passes through R₅ in the middle.
cards.10.once.soru: The two ends of a resistor are at the same potential. How much current passes through it?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: A current needs a potential difference. If V = 0, then I is 0 too.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: This is a resistor, not a shorting wire. There is no difference across the resistor's ends.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: If V = 0, then I = V/R = 0, whatever the resistance is.
cards.11.p: An ammeter measures current, is connected in series with the component, and has a very small internal resistance (the meter's own resistance). A voltmeter measures voltage, is connected in parallel, and has a very large internal resistance.
cards.11.key: No voltage drops across an ideal ammeter, and no current passes through an ideal voltmeter.
cards.12.p: The energy a source gives to each unit of charge is called emf (ε). A battery has an internal resistance (r). The terminal voltage is V = ε − I·r, and the current is I = ε/(R + r).
cards.12.key: If there is no current in the circuit, V = ε. While the battery delivers current, the terminal voltage is smaller than the emf by I·r.
cards.12.once.soru: A battery with an emf of 12 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω delivers a current of 2 A. What is the terminal voltage in V?
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: 2 V is used up in the internal resistance. So the terminal voltage is smaller than the emf.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The drop across the internal resistance is subtracted, not added.
cards.13.p: If you connect identical batteries in series, the emfs and the internal resistances add up. So n batteries give n·ε. The emf of identical batteries in parallel, however, equals that of a single battery.
cards.13.key: With batteries in parallel, the same lamp stays on longer. In this case εeq = ε and req = r/n. In series, the emf of a battery connected backward is subtracted, but its internal resistance is still added.
cards.13.once.soru: You connect three 1.5 V batteries in series. What is the total emf in V?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: In a series connection, the emfs add up: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: That would be the case in a parallel connection.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: In series, the emf is not divided. It adds up.
cards.14.p: According to the junction rule, the sum of the currents entering a point equals the sum of the currents leaving it. According to the loop rule, around a closed path the voltage of the sources equals the sum of the voltage drops across the resistors.
cards.14.key: The junction rule expresses conservation of charge, and the loop rule conservation of energy. Current is not used up in a resistor. The current leaving a resistor equals the current entering it.
cards.14.once.soru: 5 A and 3 A enter a junction and leave through a single wire. What is the outgoing current in A?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The sum of the incoming currents equals the outgoing current: 5 + 3.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Both currents enter the junction. So they are added, not subtracted.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Charge is conserved. So the 3 A must leave the junction too.
cards.15.p:
• I = q/t. Conventional current is opposite to the electrons.
• R = ρ·L/A and V = I·R.
• The slope of the V–I graph gives the resistance.
• In series the current is the same, in parallel the voltage is.
• An ammeter goes in series, a voltmeter in parallel.
• For a real battery, the terminal voltage is V = ε − I·r.
cards.15.svg#11: in parallel, Req is below the smallest resistor
cards.15.svg#12: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel
quiz.0.q: A 6 Ω resistor is connected in series with a group made of 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors in parallel. If the circuit is connected to an 18 V battery with negligible internal resistance, what is the current in the main branch in amperes?
quiz.0.e: The resistance of the parallel part is 4·12/(4 + 12) = 3 Ω. The equivalent resistance is 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, and the current is 18/9 = 2 A.
quiz.1.q: Put each property under the right type of connection.
quiz.1.ogeler.4.0: Voltage is the same across all
quiz.1.e: In a series connection, the current has a single path. The current is shared and the resistances add up. That is why an ammeter is connected in series. In a parallel connection, every branch has the same voltage and the current splits into the branches. That is why a voltmeter is connected in parallel.
quiz.2.q: A battery with an emf of 12 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across the battery's terminals in V?
quiz.2.e: The current is I = ε/(R + r) = 12/6 = 2 A. The terminal voltage is V = ε − I·r = 12 − 2·1 = 10 V. The remaining 2 V is used up inside the battery.
quiz.3.q: A metal wire is drawn out to 3 times its length without changing its volume. Since the temperature does not change, how many times its initial resistance is the wire's new resistance?
quiz.3.e: Since the volume stays constant, when the length triples the cross-sectional area drops to one third. In R = ρ·L/A, L is 3 times and A is ⅓ as large, so R becomes 9 times as large.
quiz.3.y.0: You only took the length into account. A stretched wire gets thinner, and its cross-section also drops to one third.
quiz.3.y.1: A stretched wire gets thinner. L increases and A decreases, so the resistance does not decrease. It increases.
quiz.3.y.2: Even though the volume stays constant, the length and cross-section change. Since R = ρL/A, the resistance changes too.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Close the switch, lengthen the wire, connect bulbs in series and in parallel, and solve a mixed circuit.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Electrons leave from the (−) terminal, and conventional current runs the opposite way. Close the switch.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: The circuit is complete. If 30 C of charge passes through the cross-section in 1 minute, the current is I = 30 / 60 = 0.5 A. No current forms in an open circuit.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The resistance is 4 Ω. Increase the voltage and get a current of 2 A. Use the relation V = I · R for this.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: V = I · R = 2 · 4 = 8 V. If the voltage doubles, the current doubles too. That is why the V–I graph is a straight line.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Since I = V / R, to get 2 A you need V = 2 · 4.
A:adimlar.2.metin: On a V–I graph (V vertical, I horizontal), the line's slope gives the resistance.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Which one has the larger resistance?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Y is flatter. It needs less voltage for the same current, so its resistance is small.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The slopes are different. The lines of conductors with equal resistance would lie on top of each other.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: X is steeper. It needs more voltage for the same current, so its R = V / I value is large. When they are connected in parallel, Y carries more of the current.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The resistance of a wire increases with length and decreases with cross-section. The wire is twice as long. Adjust the cross-section so that the resistance is R₀ again.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: The length doubled, and so did the cross-section. So R = 2/2 · R₀ = R₀. This is why a long extension cord is made thicker.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: The ratio L / A must be 1.
A:adimlar.4.metin: First connect the bulbs in parallel, then unscrew one bulb. Try the same with the series connection.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: When one bulb is unscrewed, in which connection does the other keep glowing?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A series connection has a single path. When one bulb is unscrewed, the circuit opens and they all go out.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In a parallel connection, each bulb has its own branch. Even if one is unscrewed, the other still gets the same 12 V (with an ideal battery) and glows just as brightly. That is why home wiring is parallel.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In a parallel connection, the path of the other branch stays open to current. You can also see in the scene that the other bulb stays on when you unscrew one.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The internal resistance of an ammeter is almost zero. You connected it in parallel with the lamp by mistake.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What happens if an ammeter is connected in parallel with a lamp?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The current skips the lamp. It passes through the ammeter, which has almost no resistance.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A path with an internal resistance of about zero has opened. The current chooses this path.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: The lamp goes out, a large current flows
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The internal resistance of an ammeter is almost zero. So a short circuit path opens across the lamp. The lamp goes out, a very large current is drawn from the battery, and the ammeter can burn out.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors connected in parallel. Adjust the battery so that 3 A flows in the main branch.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: The resistance of the parallel part is 6·3/(6+3) = 2 Ω, and the equivalent resistance is 6 Ω. So V = 3 · 6 = 18 V. 6 V drops across the parallel part. 1 A passes through the 6 Ω and 2 A through the 3 Ω, and the total is 3 A again. This is the junction rule.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: First reduce the parallel part to a single resistor: 6·3/(6+3).
A:kapanis.0: Current is the charge that passes per unit time and is found with I = q / t. Conventional current is opposite to the electrons.
A:kapanis.1: According to Ohm's law, V = I · R. The slope of the V–I graph gives the resistance.
A:kapanis.2: The resistance of a wire is found with R = ρ · L / A. A wire drawn out to twice its length has 4 times the resistance.
A:kapanis.3: In series the current is shared and Req is the sum. In parallel the voltage is shared and Req is smaller than the smallest resistor.
A:kapanis.4: An ammeter is connected in series (internal resistance ≈ 0), and a voltmeter in parallel (internal resistance very large).
